item.title: Every AI product should be working towards abstracting model choice away from users. In any product, the intelligence is the underlying engine - all the user cares about is that the job gets done. Model picking is too much cognitive load for the user. There have been multiple attempts to abstra...
item.description:
作者：Madhu Guru 账号：@realmadhuguru 简介：Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.
Every AI product should be working towards abstracting model choice away from users.
In any product, the intelligence is the underlying engine - all the user cares about is that the job gets done.
Model picking is too much cognitive load for the user.
There have been multiple attempts to abstract model choice away from users. I think we’re finally at the point where this can work well.
It takes three things:
1/ Deep understanding of the model frontier across different weight classes for your particular use cases.
2/ Great evals for your workflows, so you know which models work best where.
3/ A team with the talent and AI-native operating model to continuously adapt as the frontier moves.
Having worked with the Lovable team, I can say they have all three.

item.title: How a Professional Writer Writes With AI
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:31 Hey, it's Dan Shipper, and this week I'm excited to share a very special episode of AI and Dive. In this episode, we're previewing the release of an experimental new plugin called Compound Writing, which helps you write with AI the way that we do internally. It's inspired by Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering, and it's built by one of our staff writers, Katie Parrott. To help talk about this plugin and why Katie made it and how she uses it, Natalia Quintero is the host of this episode. She's our head of AI consulting, and she's been on the podcast a few times, and she's just an incredible interviewer.
Speaker 1 | 00:31 - 00:35 So I'm really excited for you to hear Katie and Natalia chat.
Speaker 2 | 00:49 - 01:07 Today we're talking to Katie Parrott, staff writer at Every. Katie, if if you've been following Every for a while now, will be very familiar to you. She's one of our all star writers and we're so excited to learn more about her writing process and her new plug in today.
Speaker 3 | 01:08 - 01:11 Hi Katie, how are you? I'm good. How are you?
Speaker 2 | 01:11 - 01:21 So good. I am so excited for this conversation. I am revealing myself as a Katie fangirl on on the podcast.
Speaker 3 | 01:22 - 01:23 It's a it's a mutual fandom.
Speaker 2 | 01:26 - 02:08 Thank you. Okay so Katie, almost exactly two years ago you wrote one of your most popular pieces for Every, and it was about how you had just been laid off and also maybe were in the middle of a mental health crisis, which you've written publicly about, and you decided to turn to ChatGPT as a career coach. But at the time you were also an AI skeptic, which might be crazy to think about now given some of the work that you're doing. But can you take us back to that period? What was going on in your career and in that moment in time that led you to turn to ChatTVT in the first place?
Speaker 3 | 02:08 - 02:36 Yeah. So I had just been let go from a crypto firm where I was working as an editor in Ghostwriter for the team. And, you know, that in hindsight, like it was traumatizing at the time, but in hindsight, it was like the best thing that ever happened to me because it led me back to Every. And but I was feeling really lost, as you mentioned, you know, like I had, like, tried crypto. I had tried, you know, in house.
Speaker 3 | 02:36 - 03:00 I had tried out of house. Like, I had tried all these different things. And I I felt like I was at the end of what I could do on my own, and I really needed an outside perspective. But because I was working on a budget with no clear visibility into how long I would be unemployed, hiring a real career coach wasn't really an option for me. So I had some exposure to ChatGeePTS at that time.
Speaker 3 | 03:00 - 04:18 I had actually used it, to produce briefs at a previous job as a content marketing manager. We had an agency and I realized and I was I was, like, hitting a wall of depression at that job and like could not bring myself to put words on a page. But I found that if I used ChatGPT to generate some of the repetitive stuff, And it became this assistive tool that I used as a tool for thought, which was a phrase I'd also seen Dan use around the same time, because I was following Every at the time. And so it was kind of that combination of things where I was like, okay, I can't afford like $150 an hour or however much a career coach would be, but I can sign up for a $20 a month ChatGPT subscription and get some of that same result of externalizing my thinking and getting an outside perspective and just holding me accountable for how I was thinking about my career journey and challenged me when I would get a little, like, have a tendency to catastrophize and assume the worst, and it kind of took me out of myself in that way too.
Speaker 3 | 04:18 - 04:29 And it was just, like, a really great experience for me and, like, kind of and it ultimately led me to Every. So yeah.
Speaker 2 | 04:29 - 05:06 Yeah. It's such a cool post that you wrote, and you have you just always have such great zingers in your writing that are just so delightful to read. I hope when we are sharing this on video we can pull up some of the screenshots of just what your ChatGPT prompts and screenshots look like, because it feels vintage to be looking at, you know, chat from two, two and a half years ago. But in that post you have this really great quote. It's a little lengthy, but I'm gonna try to read it because I have a question about it.
Speaker 2 | 05:06 - 05:29 So you say, One of my favorite things about writing is that I never know what I think until I write it down, but once I write it down it becomes obvious. Ultimately, what's prompting is a form of very specific strategic writing. Do I think my experiment with ChatGPT added clarity to my thinking? Yes, it has. But as with so many of these tools, the real work is still mine.
Speaker 2 | 05:29 - 06:27 Clarity, it turns out, doesn't arrive gift wrapped from a digital assistant or even a human coach. It's something I had to dig out for myself, question by question and prompt by prompt. True clarity, direction and answers come from the process of engaging with the prompts and doing the hard work yourself. AI can help guide the way, but the journey is yours to take. Just so beautiful, just so so cool, and you know I think one of the things that really resonates with me about your writing is that this feels so reflective of my experience using AI, where I attracted to the possibility of maybe an easy answer, an easy solve, but actually what I constantly find myself doing is learning something that was always there inside of me, but I had to put some work in and some clarity into to like actually get it out of me.
Speaker 2 | 06:28 - 06:40 Can you tell me a little bit more about what using AI in this very early experience and this very kind of practical high value experience, what it taught you about using AI?
Speaker 3 | 06:41 - 07:28 So the first thing it taught me is that I can use AI to to make change in my life, which is something that I've continued to carry through over the last couple of years. You know, I really judge the technology by the impact it's had practically for me. And, you know, the fact that I, you know, used the career coach, for example, I remember talking when I, like, got the invitation from Kate to write what ultimately became working overtime, my column, I was, you know, talking to ChatGPT about whether it was the right step for me to take because, I was kind of on the fence. It would have been freelancing at the time. I was kind of on the fence about that versus looking for a full time opportunity.
Speaker 3 | 07:29 - 08:01 And ChatGPT nudged me in the direction of like, well, why not try it in the mean time? And I did that, and now I'm here. And throughout my experience with AI, that's really been the thing is that it's given me both the framework for thinking, and obviously it's become the thing I think about, But it's really just about the fruits of the labor, so to speak, and seeing what AI is able to give back to me, so.
Speaker 2 | 08:01 - 09:04 So it sounds like one of the early takeaways that you had in leveraging AI was that you could really get it to be a valuable tool for you. And so that reminds me of another post that you wrote that was really popular with the Every Audience, and I believe it's titled AI turned me into a content agency of one. And early in this post, talk about how at the time you were a freelancer, so this is early twenty twenty five, and you realize that you had overcommitted yourself, or potentially overcommitted yourself, with the number of freelance projects that you had agreed to deliver. And then you go on to list the number of things that you had committed to delivering in a two week period. This includes eight blog posts, three ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts we're not even halfway through, 24 x posts, 16 Instagram posts.
